title: HOA Guide to Hiring Licensed, Insured Painters
description: What Florida HOA and condo boards should require from a painting contractor: local licensing, insurance certificates, workers’ comp, scope, and lien releases.
excerpt: The paperwork an HOA or condo board should collect before a painting crew starts, and how to compare bids fairly.
h1: The HOA Guide to Hiring Licensed, Insured Painters
heroIntro: When a community repaints, the board carries the risk. An uninsured crew, a vague scope, or a missing lien release can turn a routine project into a liability. Here is the checklist to work through before anyone sets up a ladder.

questions: What insurance should a painting contractor have for an HOA job?
Do painters need a license in Florida?
How should an HOA compare painting bids?

body: A painting project puts workers on ladders, lifts, and roofs on property the association is responsible for, next to residents’ cars, landscaping, and windows. If a worker is hurt and the contractor lacks proper coverage, or if overspray damages vehicles and the contractor cannot pay, claims can land on the association and its insurance. Collecting the right documents up front shifts that risk back where it belongs and gives the board a clear record if questions come up later. It also protects residents, who are the ones walking past the work every day, and it makes the manager’s job easier when an owner asks how the contractor was chosen.

Florida does not have a single statewide license specifically for painting contractors the way it does for roofing or general contracting. Requirements for painters are set locally and vary by county and city; some jurisdictions require a local certificate of competency or registration, and nearly all require a local business tax receipt. Ask each bidder for the license or registration that applies where your community sits, then verify it with the issuing office.

If the scope includes work beyond painting, such as structural repairs, roofing, or extensive carpentry, the contractor doing that work may need a state-certified or state-registered license. Clarify in the scope who is doing what.

bullets: Certificate of insurance (COI) showing general liability coverage, issued by the insurer or agent, with the association listed as certificate holder and named as additional insured where your governing documents or manager require it.

Workers’ compensation: Florida’s requirements for construction-industry employers are stricter than for many other businesses. Ask for proof of coverage, or a valid exemption for a sole owner, and verify it through the state’s proof-of-coverage lookup.
Commercial auto coverage for vehicles and equipment brought on site.
Any bonding the board requires, with the bond documents themselves.
Confirmation of who will actually do the work. If the contractor uses subcontractors, ask for the same documents from each one.
body: Request certificates directly from the insurance agent rather than accepting a photocopy, and check that the policy dates cover the entire project schedule.

sections.h2: A scope that can be compared
body: Bids are only comparable if they describe the same job. Before requesting proposals, have the board or manager define the scope in writing: which buildings and surfaces, what prep (washing, mildew treatment, scraping, caulking, wood and stucco repair), which product line and how many coats, color schedule, and what is excluded. Ask every bidder to respond to that scope and to include product data sheets for the primers and topcoats they propose.

Look for itemized proposals that list prep steps, products, coats, schedule, and warranty terms, and that state how unforeseen repairs such as rotted fascia will be priced and approved. Vague lump-sum bids are the most common source of disputes.

A few red flags deserve a pause: a bid far below the others with no explanation of what was left out, pressure to sign quickly, a request for most of the money before work begins, unwillingness to provide insurance certificates directly from the agent, or a proposal that names no products at all. None of these alone proves a problem, but each should prompt questions before the board votes.

Florida’s condominium and homeowners’ association statutes include competitive-bid requirements for larger contracts, and your governing documents may add their own rules. Thresholds and procedures change, so confirm current requirements with your community association manager or the association’s attorney before soliciting bids. Keep minutes that record how the contractor was selected.

Also collect a W-9, a written contract that references the scope and proposal, a payment schedule tied to completed phases rather than large upfront deposits, and a process for signed change orders. At closeout, obtain releases of lien from the contractor and, where applicable, its suppliers so unpaid vendors cannot place a lien on common property.

The best contractors plan communication as carefully as the painting. Ask bidders how they will notify residents before work begins on each building, handle vehicle relocation and overspray protection, secure ladders and materials overnight, and keep walkways safe. Multi-building projects should come with a phased schedule and a single point of contact for the manager. Exterior work in North Central Florida is best scheduled from fall through spring, with summer work planned for mornings to avoid afternoon storms.

Agree in advance on how the final punch list will work. A joint walkthrough of each building with the manager or a board representative, a written list of touch-ups, and a signed sign-off once they are completed gives everyone a clear finish line and documentation for the association’s records.

sections.h2: Build painting into the reserve plan
body: Reactive repainting is expensive. When repaint cycles are built into the reserve study and long-term maintenance plan, the board can schedule work before peeling and wood rot add repair scope. Periodic washing, annual caulk inspections, and touch-ups of the sun-exposed elevations stretch each cycle. faqs.q: Do painters need a license in Florida?
faqs.a: Florida does not issue a statewide painting contractor license. Licensing and registration for painters are handled locally and vary by county and city, so verify with the jurisdiction where the property is located.

faqs.q: What insurance should a painter have for an HOA job?
faqs.a: At minimum, general liability and workers’ compensation (or a valid exemption where allowed), plus commercial auto. Get a certificate directly from the agent naming the association as required.

faqs.q: How should an HOA compare painting bids?
faqs.a: Define the scope in writing first, then require each bidder to itemize prep, products, coats, schedule, warranty, and how unforeseen repairs are handled. Compare line by line, not just on the total.

faqs.q: What is a release of lien?
faqs.a: A document in which the contractor or supplier confirms payment and gives up the right to file a construction lien on the property. Collect them at closeout.
